summary: Describes how an IPv4 host can detect an address conflict, where two hosts on the same link use the same address. It provides a precaution a host can take before using an address and a way to notice conflicts afterward. It is a standards-track specification.

plainLanguage.summary: If two kids on a team get the same jersey number, the referee gets confused. This tells computers to check first and to notice if a duplicate appears.

questions: what is ipv4 address conflict detection
how does a host defend its ip address
subtitle: How an IPv4 host checks, with ARP, that nobody else is using its address, and what it does if someone is.

tldr.problem: Two hosts on the same link using the same IPv4 address cause hard-to-diagnose failures, and the DHCP specification gave no detail on how to check for this.
tldr.mechanism: Before using an address, a host broadcasts ARP Probes, then sends ARP Announcements. While it keeps the address, it watches every ARP packet for another host claiming it and then gives up, defends, or reports.
tldr.outcome: RFC 5227 is a Proposed Standard that updates RFC 826. It works for any way an address was configured, and IPv4 Link-Local addressing can be seen as a special case of it.

facts.label: Minimum link speed
facts.value: 1 Mb/s, round trip at most one second

today: RFC 5227 is a Proposed Standard. It updates RFC 826 and, according to the unit metadata, has not been obsoleted or updated by a later RFC.

sections.title: The Duplicate Address Problem
sections.content:
Accidentally giving two hosts the same IP address has often been an annoying and hard-to-diagnose problem. The Address Resolution Protocol (RFC 826) already gives a host an easy way to notice it, and the DHCP specification (RFC 2131) says in passing that a client SHOULD probe a new address, for example with ARP.

What DHCP does not say is how many ARP packets to send, how far apart, how long to wait, which packets to listen for, or what to do if a conflict turns up later. RFC 5227 fills those gaps with IPv4 Address Conflict Detection (ACD).

The mechanism is not tied to DHCP. However an address was configured (typed by a person, handed out by a DHCP server or chosen by other software), detecting conflicts is useful. The configuring agent is told about the error and may stop using the network or pick a new address.
sections.plainLanguage: If two houses on a street get the same number, the mail goes to the wrong place. This RFC tells computers exactly how to check for that before they move in, and what to do if it happens anyway.

sections.title: ARP Probes, Announcements and Timing Constants
sections.content:
RFC 5227 does not change the ARP packet format or any rule in RFC 826. It only gives two special uses of an ARP Request their own names.

An ARP Probe is an ARP Request broadcast on the local link with an all-zero sender IP address. The sender hardware address MUST be the sending interface's address, and the target IP address MUST be the address being probed. The sender IP is zero so that other hosts' ARP caches are not polluted if the address turns out to be in use. A probe asks "Is anyone using this address?" and implies "This is the address I hope to use."

An ARP Announcement is the same packet except that both the sender and target IP address fields hold the address being announced. It says "This is the address I am now using."

The timing values are fixed constants, not tunables, and are listed in the table below.

The constants have symbolic names only so that future standards could refer to this document with different values. At the time of writing, no such standards exist.
sections.plainLanguage: A probe is asking the room "Is this seat taken?" without saying who you are. An announcement is standing up and saying "This seat is mine now!"

sections.title: Probing and Announcing an Address
sections.content:
Before using an IPv4 address, however it was obtained, a host MUST test whether it is already in use by broadcasting ARP Probes. This also applies when an interface goes from inactive to active, when a computer wakes from sleep, when a cable is connected, when a wireless interface associates with a new base station, or on any other change that makes the host actively connected to a link. A host MUST NOT do this check periodically, because that wastes bandwidth and passive detection (see below) makes it unnecessary.

The host first waits a random time between zero and PROBE_WAIT (1 second), then sends PROBE_NUM (3) probes, spaced randomly between PROBE_MIN (1 second) and PROBE_MAX (2 seconds) apart. The random delay keeps many hosts that power on together from probing at the same instant.

From the start of probing until ANNOUNCE_WAIT (2 seconds) after the last probe, any ARP packet (Request or Reply) whose sender IP is the probed address means the address is in use, and the host MUST treat it that way and tell the configuring agent. A host SHOULD also treat an ARP Probe for the same target address from a different hardware address as a conflict, which covers two hosts probing at the same moment. The hardware-address check matters because some repeaters and wireless access points rebroadcast packets back to their sender.

If no conflict appears by ANNOUNCE_WAIT seconds after the last probe, the address may be used safely. The host MUST then broadcast ANNOUNCE_NUM (2) ARP Announcements, ANNOUNCE_INTERVAL (2 seconds) apart, so that other hosts drop stale cache entries left by a previous holder of the address. It may start using the address right after the first announcement.
sections.plainLanguage: You wait a random moment, ask "Is this seat taken?" three times, and listen. If nobody says anything, you sit down and tell the whole room twice that the seat is yours.

sections.title: Ongoing Detection and Defending the Address
sections.content:
Conflict detection does not stop once the address is in use. If a host ever receives an ARP packet (Request or Reply) whose sender IP is its own address but whose sender hardware address is not one of its own, another host thinks it owns the address. The host MUST respond in one of three ways.

  • (a) Give up. It MAY stop using the address at once and signal an error to the configuring agent.
  • (b) Defend once. If it has active TCP connections or other reasons to keep the address and has seen no other conflicting packet within DEFEND_INTERVAL (10 seconds), it MAY record the time and broadcast a single ARP Announcement. If a second conflict arrives within DEFEND_INTERVAL seconds, it MUST stop using the address and signal an error, so two hosts do not defend forever.
  • (c) Defend indefinitely. A device that must never give up its address, such as a link's default router or a DNS server, MAY keep defending. It logs details such as the source Ethernet address, informs an administrator at a controlled rate, and MUST NOT send another defensive announcement within DEFEND_INTERVAL seconds of the last one.

A host that wants reliable operation MUST do one of these; ignoring conflicting packets gives seemingly random failures that are hard to diagnose. Before abandoning an address a host SHOULD actively try to reset existing connections using it. From its first announcement until it stops using the address, the host MUST keep answering ARP Requests for it in the usual RFC 826 way, including probes.
sections.plainLanguage: If someone else claims your seat while you are sitting in it, you can leave, say "this is mine" once, or, if you are the teacher, keep insisting and tell the principal. But two kids must not shout at each other forever.

sections.title: Rate Limiting, Links and Broadcast Replies
sections.content:
To prevent ARP storms from failures such as a DHCP server that keeps assigning the same address to everyone, a host that has seen MAX_CONFLICTS (10) or more conflicts on an interface MUST try no more than one new address per RATE_LIMIT_INTERVAL (60 seconds). This covers conflicts found while probing and conflicts found later.

The specification applies to IEEE 802 LANs and to other link technologies running at least 1 Mb/s, with a round-trip latency of at most one second, that use ARP. Slower links still work but may see more late conflicts, and different values for the probe, announce and rate-limit parameters may be wanted there. Hosts need not all implement ACD or use the same timings: a protected host only needs its peers to answer ARP Requests correctly as RFC 826 requires. ACD detects conflicts only on the same physical link, which is correct, since a private address like 10.0.0.1 is legitimately used on countless separate networks.

Normally ARP Replies are unicast, so if two hosts A and B share an address, a third host C sees both replies but A and B do not see each other's. Sending replies by link-level broadcast detects such conflicts sooner but raises broadcast traffic by at most a factor of two. RFC 5227 says this is NOT RECOMMENDED for general use, though RFC 3927 uses it for IPv4 Link-Local addresses.
sections.plainLanguage: If you keep picking seats that are already taken, you have to slow down and wait a minute between tries so you do not make a racket. Shouting every answer to the whole room finds clashes faster, but it makes more noise.

sections.title: Why Requests, and Why Gratuitous ARP Is Not Enough
sections.content:
The RFC asks why announcements use ARP Request packets rather than "gratuitous" ARP Replies. It gives two reasons. The historical one: Gratuitous ARP as documented by Stevens uses ARP Requests, and BSD Unix, Microsoft Windows, Mac OS 9 and Mac OS X all follow that, so mandating a switch would be futile. The practical one: a faulty ARP implementation is more likely to reject an unsolicited Reply (for example one that arrives by broadcast or whose target fields do not match) than a Request.

The historical note also rejects the claim that Gratuitous ARP already provides duplicate address detection. It sends only a single announcement when an interface is configured, so the existing holder logs an error while the newcomer carries on, and both hosts end up resetting each other's TCP connections. The probing and defence steps in RFC 5227 help a host stay robust even when the other host does not follow the same rules.
sections.plainLanguage: Shouting "I live here!" once when you move in is not the same as checking whether someone already lives there. This RFC adds the checking part.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
ACD is built on ARP and inherits its weaknesses. A malicious host can send fraudulent ARP packets, for example answering every ARP Request with its own hardware address and so claiming every address on the network.

The RFC says its mechanism makes this existing weakness no worse, and in some ways better, since hosts now reconfigure or at least inform the user instead of failing silently. There is one new risk: if a host picks a new address after a conflict (option (a)), an attacker on the same link could find it easier to hijack TCP connections. Actively resetting existing connections before abandoning an address helps mitigate that.
sections.plainLanguage: Anyone in the room can lie and say "that seat is mine." This RFC does not stop liars, but it does make sure you notice something is wrong instead of being confused.

messages.label: ARP Probe x3
messages.note: Broadcast ARP Request with all-zero sender IP, target is the address wanted. Spaced 1 to 2 seconds apart.

messages.note: Sent 2 seconds apart after no conflict was seen, with sender and target IP both set to the chosen address.
